notes: Compulsory purchase disturbance appeal; freed-up time deduction overturned on procedural fairness and evidential grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Compulsory purchase compensation: freed-up time deduction overturned
key_facts: Brian Faraday claimed disturbance compensation after Carmarthenshire County Council compulsorily acquired his commercial property at 10 Island Place, Llanelli, where he ran an estate agency.
The Lands Tribunal found the compulsory purchase scheme had caused loss of business profits from the early 1980s but reduced the award by 25% to 50% to reflect Mr Faraday's allegedly freed-up time.
Neither party had argued for a freed-up time deduction and no evidence addressed how Mr Faraday could have used spare time profitably.
The tribunal otherwise held Mr Faraday had mitigated his loss reasonably and awarded total compensation of about £354,111 plus interest, including a £66,345 freed-up time deduction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Lands Tribunal decision on compulsory purchase disturbance compensation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the £66,345 freed-up time deduction restored to the compensation award together with agreed interest; no remittal to the tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal may not reduce compulsory purchase disturbance compensation for freed-up time where the point was not raised by the parties, was not explored in evidence, and lacked a proper evidential foundation; even if mitigation by use of spare time could in exceptional cases reduce compensation, that was not established here and procedural fairness required the parties be given an opportunity to address any new point.
legal_issues: Whether compensation for loss of business profits may be reduced for freed-up time
Whether the Lands Tribunal erred procedurally in raising the point without notice
Whether the deduction was a matter of mitigation or loss quantification
Whether the case should be remitted for further findings on freed-up time

notes: Ex parte trade mark injunction discharged for non-disclosure of other Bangla cards on the market.

enrichment.short_title: Bangla telephone card ex parte injunction discharged for non-disclosure
key_facts: Alma Communications and Neutron Marketing sought to continue an ex parte injunction restraining Feedback Communications from using the mark Bangla on telephone cards.
The claimants relied on a Community trade mark and passing off in relation to the Bangla mark and get-up featuring a world map.
Material not disclosed to Lloyd J or Laddie J showed correspondence from January 2004 and at least four other Bangla-branded cards already on the market.
The claimants had sent cease-and-desist letters to some other users but had not pursued them further.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Inter partes application to continue ex parte injunctive relief originally granted without notice.
enrichment.outcome: The ex parte injunction was not continued in any form pending the inter partes hearing.
enrichment.ratio: A party seeking ex parte relief must make full and frank disclosure of material going to the heart of entitlement to relief; failure to disclose that substantially identical marks were already used by others on the market is a profound breach of that duty and makes continuation of ex parte relief inappropriate even if the defendants do not oppose a narrower injunction.
legal_issues: Whether ex parte injunctive relief should be continued
Whether the claimants breached the duty of full and frank disclosure
Effect of existing third-party use of the Bangla mark on the claimants' case

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment with a clear outcome driven by undisclosed market facts; merits of the trade mark claim were not finally decided.

notes: Exxon Valdez retrocession trial; English law governs and clean-up costs fall outside inward Section I cover.

enrichment.short_title: Exxon Valdez reinsurance retrocession coverage under English law
key_facts: Following the 1989 Exxon Valdez grounding and massive Alaskan oil spill, Exxon incurred very large clean-up and liability costs.
Claimant reinsurers sought recovery from retrocessionaires under excess-of-loss retrocession contracts aggregating thousands of inward claims.
The dispute concerned coverage under Exxon's GCE primary policies, especially Sections I, IIIA and IIIB, and whether English or New York law governed.
Pollution exclusions in outward retrocession contracts were also in issue, including seepage and pollution clauses excluding offshore-origin contamination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of coverage issues under reinsurance and retrocession contracts arising from the Exxon Valdez disaster.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the retrocessionaires on the English law analysis: the primary policies were governed by English law; oil pollution clean-up was not covered under Section I and related recovery routes failed, with pollution exclusions also excluding liability under many outward contracts; alternative New York law analysis would have produced a different partial outcome but still limited retrocession recovery.
enrichment.ratio: On the proper law analysis the Exxon GCE primary policies were governed by English law; Exxon's oil pollution clean-up expenditure was not within Section I cover and, in any event, notwithstanding clauses and pollution exclusions prevented the retrocessionaires' liability; ESC's expenses could not be included in ultimate net loss because the 1996 Section I settlement did not settle ESC claims and any ESC claim was time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether the primary insurance policies were governed by English or New York law
Whether Exxon's clean-up costs were covered under Section I, IIIA or IIIB
Whether pollution and notwithstanding clauses excluded recovery
Whether ESC expenses formed part of ultimate net loss under the retrocession
How New York law would have applied if relevant

notes: Trade mark appeal dismissed; COCO element in COCO DE MER likely to confuse for identical luxury goods.

enrichment.short_title: Chanel opposition to COCO DE MER trade mark registration upheld
key_facts: Coco de Mer Limited applied to register COCO DE MER for perfumery, jewellery, bags and clothing for its erotic retail business in Covent Garden.
Chanel opposed registration relying on its established COCO mark used on perfumes, toiletries and fashion goods worldwide.
The hearing officer upheld the opposition under section 5(2)(b) on likelihood of association and confusion because COCO was a strong element of the applied-for mark.
Chanel did not rely on section 5(4)(a) as providing any stronger basis than section 5(2)(b).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court from a Trade Marks Registry hearing officer decision refusing registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; registration refused on likelihood of confusion under section 5(2)(b).
enrichment.ratio: Where identical or highly similar classes of luxury goods are involved, the strong and distinctive COCO element in COCO DE MER is likely to cause the average consumer to associate the marks and believe the goods come from the same or economically linked undertakings, even though DE MER and the device add some dissimilarity; the global assessment required by ECJ authorities supports the hearing officer's conclusion.
legal_issues: Degree of similarity between COCO and COCO DE MER
Distinctive character of the earlier COCO mark
Likelihood of confusion including association for identical goods
Whether GIORGIO BEVERLY HILLS required a different outcome
Proper application of the section 5(2) composite question

notes: Leading Court of Appeal guidance on ADR refusals and costs; both Halsey and Steel appeals dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: When refusal of mediation may affect costs of successful parties
key_facts: In Halsey, a widow's clinical negligence claim against Milton Keynes NHS Trust was dismissed after the Trust repeatedly refused mediation on a low-value disputed claim.
In Steel, the second defendant successfully resisted a Part 20 contribution claim and refused a late invitation to mediate a legal issue about overlapping spinal injury damage.
Four interveners, including the Law Society and Civil Mediation Council, made detailed submissions on ADR and costs.
The court also held in Steel that Performance Cars remained good law and the second accident did not cause the same long-term damage as the first.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two conjoined appeals to the Court of Appeal raising when a successful litigant may be deprived of costs for refusing ADR, plus a Part 20 causation appeal in Steel.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; comprehensive guidance given that courts may encourage but not compel ADR, and costs sanctions against successful parties require the unsuccessful party to show unreasonable refusal; neither unsuccessful party discharged that burden.
enrichment.ratio: Compulsion of unwilling parties to mediate would likely violate article 6 ECHR access to court; when considering costs, the burden is on the unsuccessful party to show the successful party unreasonably refused ADR, having regard to factors including the nature of the dispute, merits, other settlement attempts, disproportionate mediation cost, delay, and prospects of success, without treating ADR as presumptively required or giving special weight to the government ADR pledge.
legal_issues: Whether courts may order unwilling parties to mediate
When a successful party's refusal of ADR justifies a costs penalty
Relevant factors in assessing unreasonable refusal of mediation
Whether public bodies should be treated differently on costs
In Steel, whether the second tortfeasor was liable for the same accelerated spinal damage

Hurst v Leeming [2001] EWHC 1051 (Ch)
R (Cowl) v Plymouth City Council [2001] EWCA Civ 1935
Performance Cars Ltd v Abraham [1962] 1 QB 33

notes: Revenue challenge to Wimbledon FC CVA dismissed; Football Creditors paid by purchaser under League policy.

enrichment.short_title: Wimbledon FC company voluntary arrangement survives Revenue challenge

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: Hopelessly insolvent Wimbledon Football Club entered administration in June 2003 and agreed to sell its undertaking and Football League share to Milton Keynes Dons Limited.
The Football League's insolvency policy required Football Creditors and certain other debts to be paid in full as a condition of retaining league membership.

Creditors approved a company voluntary arrangement paying preferential creditors, including the Inland Revenue, 30 pence in the pound while non-preferential Football Creditors would be paid 100 pence in the pound by the buyer.
The Revenue applied to revoke or suspend the CVA for material irregularity under section 4(4)(a) and unfair prejudice under section 6.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited section 6 Insolvency Act application to revoke or suspend approval of a company voluntary arrangement.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the CVA was not materially irregular and did not unfairly prejudice the Revenue, with relief in any event refused in the court's discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Section 4(4)(a) requires preferential creditors to be paid ahead of non-preferential creditors only from the company's assets, not from third parties paying non-preferential Football Creditors out of their own money at commercial necessity; where the only alternative to the CVA was liquidation with nil return, differential treatment securing a going-concern sale did not unfairly prejudice preferential creditors.
legal_issues: Whether payment of Football Creditors in full by the buyer breached section 4(4)(a)
Whether the CVA unfairly prejudiced the Revenue
Whether objection lay to the sale agreement rather than the CVA
Whether the court should exercise its discretion to revoke the arrangement
linked_authorities: Peck v Craighead [1995] BCLC 337
Cazaly Irving Holdings Ltd v Cancol Ltd [1996] BPIR 252
Sea Voyager Maritime Inc v Bielecki [1999] 1 All ER 628
Business City Express Ltd [1997] BCC 826

notes: Hire-purchase appeal dismissed; company buyer treated as consumer and defective Lamborghini validly rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Company hire-purchaser as consumer rejects defective Lamborghini
area_of_law: Sale of goods and supply of services

statutes_considered.title: Sale and Supply of Goods (Implied Terms) Act 1973

key_facts: Feldarol Foundry plc hire-purchased a Lamborghini Diablo for its managing director through Hermes Leasing.
The car had serious steering and brake defects and potentially unsafe handling, though repairable for about £1,000.
Mr Beresford returned the car to the dealer in July 2002 and later notified the finance company that the car had been rejected.
The finance company relied on exclusion clauses and argued the company was not dealing as a consumer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from county court findings on consumer status, satisfactory quality, exclusion clauses, rejection and affirmation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the company was dealing as a consumer, the car was not of satisfactory quality, rejection was effective and the contract was not affirmed.
enrichment.ratio: A company buying a director's luxury car as an occasional perquisite rather than as a regular integral part of its business may deal as a consumer under section 12 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 following R & B Customs Brokers, which remains binding; serious steering and brake defects breach the section 10 satisfactory quality term and early return and rejection communications showed the hirer had not affirmed the agreement.
legal_issues: Whether a company can deal as consumer under section 12 UCTA 1977
Whether exclusion clauses were effective or reasonable
Whether the car was of satisfactory quality
Whether the hirer rejected or affirmed the hire-purchase agreement

notes: Forward sale default clause construed to require valuation at termination, not delayed asset sales.

enrichment.short_title: Socimer forward sale agreement default valuation at termination date
key_facts: Socimer International Bank and Standard Bank London entered a 1996 umbrella agreement governing forward sale transactions in emerging market debt instruments.
After Socimer defaulted and entered liquidation in 1998, its liquidator claimed Standard should account for surplus value of designated assets exceeding unpaid amounts.
Standard contended it could sell designated assets over time after default and apply actual proceeds against Socimer's debts.
The preliminary issue concerned construction of clause 14 events-of-default provisions and whether valuation crystallised at termination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a preliminary issue on the construction of an events-of-default clause in a forward sale agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Socimer on construction; Standard was obliged to value designated assets as at the termination date and could not rely on later sale proceeds for the clause 14 accounting.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 14(a)(bb) of the forward sale agreement requires the net position between buyer and seller to be crystallised at or immediately after termination by valuing designated assets as at the termination date, with Standard's broad discretion operating within a valuation exercise rather than permitting indefinite delayed sales at the seller's risk to Socimer's detriment; the second sentence fixing value on the date of termination cannot be ignored or blue-pencilled.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 14 events-of-default in a forward sale agreement
Whether Standard could sell assets after termination and apply later proceeds
Relationship between liquidation/retention options and termination-date valuation
Application of commercial/common-sense principles to financial contracts

Mannai Investment Co Ltd v Eagle Star Life Assurance Co Ltd [1997] 3 All ER 352
Rank Xerox Ltd v Gerard [2001] EWCA Civ 415

notes: Pain/gain sub-contract issue partly resolved; sub-contract found but sharing mechanism still to be determined by the court.

enrichment.short_title: Alstom-Jarvis Metro sub-contract pain and gain mechanism unresolved
key_facts: Alstom was main contractor to Railtrack on the Sunderland Direct Project to extend the Tyne and Wear Metro.
Jarvis performed part of the works under a sub-contract derived from Issue 3 contract documents.
The main contract included a target-cost pain/gain incentive scheme linked to Railtrack's agreed target price.
Alstom sought a declaration that Jarvis had agreed to share pain and gain, while Jarvis accepted pain/gain sharing in principle but disputed the mechanism.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court claim for declarations on whether the sub-contract included a pain/gain sharing mechanism and related pricing issues.
enrichment.outcome: Partial decision only: the court found a sub-contract concluded in 2002 on Issue 3 terms with clause 45.3 dispute resolution, and that Jarvis agreed in principle to pain/gain sharing but no specific mechanism was agreed; further submissions invited before final determination of the outstanding difference.
enrichment.ratio: Where sub-contract documents show Jarvis unequivocally accepted participation in pain/gain sharing but the parties never agreed the operative mechanism, the court may determine that outstanding difference under clause 45.3, but on the evidence no concluded agreement on the mechanism had yet been reached.
legal_issues: Whether a sub-contract was concluded on Issue 3 terms
Whether the sub-contract included a pain/gain sharing obligation
What mechanism should apply to share main contract pain or gain
Whether the court should determine the outstanding difference under clause 45.3

notes: LPG fleet SPA summary judgment on expert determination and good faith; some declarations and costs still to be finalised.

enrichment.short_title: Tarquin LPG fleet sale: expert determination and SPA construction
key_facts: Bernhard Schulte sellers agreed to sell eleven LPG carriers constituting the Tarquin Fleet to Nile Holdings purchasers under an April 2002 sale and purchase agreement.
The SPA provided for expert determination of price adjustments where purchasers identified defects affecting vessel value after inspection.
Disputes arose over whether references to the expert were made in time under clauses 3.3 and 3.4, the valuation date for price reduction, alleged expert bias, and breach of good faith duties.
The sellers counterclaimed for breach of confidentiality and good faith; purchasers sought to uphold the expert's determinations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications for summary judgment and declarations on construction of an ship sale and purchase agreement and an expert determination process.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed interim outcome in draft judgment: sellers entitled to declarations that expert references were out of time and price reduction was based on inspection-date condition; purchasers entitled to several declarations upholding compliance and limiting challenges to the expert; summary judgment for purchasers on good faith counterclaim; further issues on waiver/estoppel and final orders reserved.
enrichment.ratio: On proper construction of the SPA, price-adjustment references to the expert must be made within clause 3.3's time limit and the expert's reduction in price is assessed by reference to vessel condition at inspection; expert determinations are binding absent manifest procedural unfairness, while a separate breach-of-good-faith claim may succeed against sellers where supported on the pleaded facts.
legal_issues: Construction of clauses 3.3 and 3.4 time limits for expert references
Whether the expert's valuation date was the inspection date
Whether the expert's determinations were challengeable for bias or procedural unfairness
Whether purchasers breached good faith or confidentiality duties
Whether summary judgment should be granted on remaining claims

confidence.notes: Judgment was delivered in draft with several declarations indicated but final orders, summary judgment scope and costs still subject to further submissions.
